# **Motivation**
***

Lupus is an {{< glossary "Autoimmune disease" display="autoimmune disease" >}} in which the body mounts an immune response against its own tissues [@niams_lupus_overview]. The @lfa2025lupusFacts estimates that 1.5 million Americans live with some form of the disease. While lupus can affect anyone, some populations are more affected than others. In this case study, we will focus on {{< glossary "Systemic lupus erythematosus" display="systemic lupus erythematosus" >}} (SLE), the most common type, accounting for approximately 70% of lupus cases [@lfa2025lupusFacts]. SLE can be challenging to study because the affected tissues and experienced symptoms can vary strikingly between individuals and over time [@niams_lupus_overview]. The {{< glossary "Gene expression profile" display="gene expression profiles" >}} of blood immune cells provide an accessible window into some aspects of the immune activity associated with SLE [@catalina2019interferonSLE]. However, gene expression within a cell may reflect different influences, including expression related to helping that cell function as the type of cell that it is, as well as gene expression related to immune related activity including {{< glossary "Immune signaling" display="immune signaling" >}}, as well as differences between individuals, such as differences in the severity of their SLE [@kang2018multiplexed].

![Lupus can affect several tissues, with symptoms that vary between people and over time. The 1.5-million estimate covers all forms of lupus, not only SLE [@niams_lupus_overview; @lfa2025lupusFacts]. Illustrations adapted from NIH BioArt (Ryan Kissinger), Health Icons, and Avataaars (Pablo Stanley; Fang-Pen Lin). See Acknowledgments for artwork credits.](img/motivation_lupus_comic.png){#fig-motivation-lupus fig-alt="Four-panel comic about lupus. An immune response targets the body's own tissues. Symptoms include fatigue, skin rash, joint pain and possible organ involvement, and can vary over time. A panel attributes the estimate of 1.5 million Americans with some form of lupus to the Lupus Foundation of America. The final panel shows how changing symptoms, illness and care costs can disrupt daily life." width=900 .lightbox title=""}

Latent-variable analysis offers one way to investigate this complexity. A {{< glossary "Latent variable" display="latent variable" >}} is a feature that we do not measure directly but infer from observed data [@johnson2023cogapsWorkflow]. In this case study, we will use {{< glossary "CoGAPS" >}} to investigate how blood immune cells respond to {{< glossary "IFN-beta" display="interferon-beta" >}} (IFN-beta), an immune system signaling protein [@catalina2019interferonSLE]. We will compare {{< glossary "Gene expression" display="gene expression" >}} in IFN-beta-stimulated and untreated cells from the same {{< glossary "Donor" display="donors" >}} [@kang2018multiplexed]. We will look for responses shared across cell types and patterns associated with differences in {{< glossary "Immune-cell identity" display="cell identity" >}}.

![Gene-expression profiles can reflect overlapping influences, including cell identity and response to stimulation. CoGAPS infers patterns that researchers evaluate using contributing genes and cell activities [@kang2018multiplexed; @johnson2023cogapsWorkflow]. The conditions contain different cells from the same donors; the diagrams are conceptual, not fitted results. Researcher illustration adapted from Avataaars (Pablo Stanley; Fang-Pen Lin). See Acknowledgments for artwork credits.](img/motivation_immune_cell_patterns_comic.png){#fig-motivation-immune-cell-patterns fig-alt="Four-panel comic showing untreated and IFN-beta-stimulated samples from the same donors, with T cells, B cells and monocytes. Overlapping colored layers represent cell identity and stimulation effects on gene expression. CoGAPS infers patterns from an expression matrix. A researcher then examines contributing genes and compares cell activities to ask whether a response is shared. All grids, colors and patterns are schematic." width=900 .lightbox title=""}

Similar questions arise in other areas of research, where cells can share a biological response while retaining their distinct identities. CoGAPS has been used to investigate cell types and developmental processes in the mouse retina [@steinobrien2019transferLearning], to examine {{< glossary "Neural development" display="neural development" >}} [@kim2024neuralFates], and to examine immune-cell states associated with {{< glossary "Cancer immunotherapy" display="cancer immunotherapy" >}} [@davismarcisak2021nkActivation]. You can apply this approach in your own research to identify genes associated with each pattern and compare pattern activity across cell types and experimental conditions [@johnson2023cogapsWorkflow].
